what_it_does: Chip designers need tools that can automatically check whether a hardware design is correct and secure before it is manufactured. One powerful technique is symbolic execution: instead of running the chip on one specific input, the tool reasons about all possible inputs at once by treating them as mathematical symbols, then hands the resulting logical constraints to a solver program. The problem is an explosion of paths — when a circuit has many branching conditions, the number of symbolic paths grows exponentially, making full verification impractically slow. SYLQ-SV addresses this by caching the answers to logical queries: if the tool encounters a constraint it has already solved (even on a different path through the circuit), it reuses the saved answer rather than invoking the solver again. The system is built specifically for SystemVerilog — the industry-standard language used to describe chip blueprints — and supports a formal assertion language called SVA, making it applicable to real open-source hardware designs.
